    To Escape Illinois’ Swipe-Fee Law, Open a Branch in Illinois

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that few charges draw complaints from as many directions as the card swipe fee.
    • In a recent development, few charges draw complaints from as many directions as the card swipe fee.
    • Under that pressure, states have begun tiptoeing toward regulating interchange fees, or swipe fees, themselves.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that few charges draw complaints from as many directions as the card swipe fee. Merchants resent the cut that card-issuing banks and payment networks take from every sale, and consumers resent checkout fees for paying by credit card.Under that pressure, states have begun tiptoeing toward regulating interchange fees, or swipe fees, themselves. The first to act, Illinois, reads federal banking law in a way that lets an out-of-state bank escape its rules only by opening a physical branch there. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. has rightly proposed a rule to end that absurdity.Illinois’ Interchange Fee Prohibition Act, set to take effect in July 2027, bars banks from collecting swipe fees on the sales tax and tip portion of a purchase. But federal law exempts national banks from this kind of state regulation, and Congress extended this protection to state-chartered banks to create parity.Illinois reads that protection as covering only those with a physical branch in the state. A small bank in Iowa serving Illinois customers from across the line may have to comply; an identical institution with an Illinois branch is exempt.>>> The Debanking Scandal Started in Washington, Not Wall StreetThat’s wrong, and the FDIC is right to try to fix it.States have a legitimate, long-standing role in protecting consumers and regulating commerce within their borders. But the Constitution gives Congress the power to regulate commerce among the states, and for good reason. Without a strong defense of Commerce Clause principles, a few states can bully the rest into following their rules. For multi-state banks, Congress has already set a reasonable standard.Anyone who has worked on state policy, as I did in Arizona, knows the governing principle: in-state presence. An out-of-state business with a substantial in-state presence—such as a physical location—answers to that state’s rules.When the Supreme Court’s 2018 Wayfair decision let states require remote sellers to collect sales tax, the fight was over whether less than a physical presence could count. Nobody ever suggested opening a store in Arizona would exempt a seller from its sales tax.Illinois’ reading of federal banking law produces exactly that absurd result. The provision at issue, from the Riegle-Neal Act, refers to out-of-state banks’ “branches” in the host state, and Illinois reads that word as a limit. Approve a card purchase for a customer passing through Illinois, with no physical location there, and Illinois may say you are subject to its law. Open a branch, and suddenly you are exempt.The result is a regulatory reach that shrinks as a bank’s presence grows. The few state banks based outside Illinois but with a branch there would be exempt, while the 3,185 state banks the FDIC identifies as potentially affected (most of them small) would not. Those banks could spend the resources to comply, but to get an exemption, they would perversely have to open a branch there.That’s not what Congress set out to do. Riegle-Neal was a law about interstate banking and branching, written when banks served customers through branches and the first iPhone was more than a decade away. When Congress amended it in 1997, the bill’s sponsor was plain about the goal: “The essence of this legislation is to provide parity between state-chartered banks and national banks.”Turning a word that described 1990s banking into a penalty on modern remote service banking gets that purpose backward and destroys parity.>>> The Fed Got It Right; Now Congress Must Do the SameThe FDIC’s proposal applies the sensible reading. Where a host state’s law does not apply to an out-of-state national bank, it does not apply to an out-of-state state bank either, branch or no branch. The rule does not replace state regulation with federal regulation; it restores common sense and legislative intent to a 1990s-era statute.If anything, Illinois’ reading works against state authority. The dual banking system, which lets a bank choose a state or federal charter, is itself an expression of federalism. Make the state charter the costlier one, and, as the FDIC observes, banks could shift to federal charters. That would be a strange victory indeed for states’ rights.It also would be an expensive one. The FDIC estimates the affected state banks would spend about $308 million up front and nearly $7 million a year complying, all to transfer roughly $2.3 million a year in fees from banks to merchants. With 11 other states having explored similar legislation, the problem is unlikely to stay in Illinois.If federal law has gone too far or failed to account for state needs in a card-dependent, network-based economy, it’s Congress’ job to amend it. But no reasonable reading of that framework would exempt a bank for moving into a state while penalizing its competitor for staying home.The FDIC has proposed saying that clearly. It should finalize the rule. A bank shouldn’t have to move into Illinois to get out from under Illinois law.

    In a recent development, few charges draw complaints from as many directions as the card swipe fee. Merchants resent the cut that card-issuing banks and payment networks take from every sale, and consumers resent checkout fees for paying by credit card.

    Under that pressure, states have begun tiptoeing toward regulating interchange fees, or swipe fees, themselves. The first to act, Illinois, reads federal banking law in a way that lets an out-of-state bank escape its rules only by opening a physical branch there. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. has rightly proposed a rule to end that absurdity.

    Illinois’ Interchange Fee Prohibition Act, set to take effect in July 2027, bars banks from collecting swipe fees on the sales tax and tip portion of a purchase. But federal law exempts national banks from this kind of state regulation, and Congress extended this protection to state-chartered banks to create parity.

    Illinois reads that protection as covering only those with a physical branch in the state. A small bank in Iowa serving Illinois customers from across the line may have to comply; an identical institution with an Illinois branch is exempt.

    >>> The Debanking Scandal Started in Washington, Not Wall Street.

    That’s wrong, and the FDIC is right to try to fix it.

    Industry observers note that states have a legitimate, long-standing role in protecting consumers and regulating commerce within their borders. But the Constitution gives Congress the power to regulate commerce among the states, and for good reason. Without a strong defense of Commerce Clause principles, a few states can bully the rest into following their rules. For multi-state banks, Congress has already set a reasonable standard.

    Sources indicate that anyone who has worked on state policy, as I did in Arizona, knows the governing principle: in-state presence. An out-of-state business with a substantial in-state presence—such as a physical location—answers to that state’s rules.

    Industry observers note that when the Supreme Court’s 2018 Wayfair decision let states require remote sellers to collect sales tax, the fight was over whether less than a physical presence could count. Nobody ever suggested opening a store in Arizona would exempt a seller from its sales tax.

    Illinois’ reading of federal banking law produces exactly that absurd result. The provision at glitch, from the Riegle-Neal Act, refers to out-of-state banks’ “branches” in the host state, and Illinois reads that word as a limit. Approve a card purchase for a customer passing through Illinois, with no physical location there, and Illinois may say you are subject to its law. Open a branch, and suddenly you are exempt.

    Sources indicate that the result is a regulatory reach that shrinks as a bank’s presence grows. The few state banks based outside Illinois but with a branch there would be exempt, while the 3,185 state banks the FDIC identifies as potentially affected (most of them small) would not. Those banks could spend the resources to comply, but to get an exemption, they would perversely have to open a branch there.

    That’s not what Congress set out to do. Riegle-Neal was a law about interstate banking and branching, written when banks served customers through branches and the first iPhone was more than a decade away. When Congress amended it in 1997, the bill’s sponsor was plain about the goal: “The essence of this legislation is to provide parity between state-chartered banks and national banks.”.

    Turning a word that described 1990s banking into a penalty on modern remote service banking gets that purpose backward and destroys parity.

    >>> The Fed Got It Right; Now Congress Must Do the Same.

    Sources indicate that the FDIC’s proposal applies the sensible reading. Where a host state’s law does not apply to an out-of-state national bank, it does not apply to an out-of-state state bank either, branch or no branch. The rule does not replace state regulation with federal regulation; it restores common sense and legislative intent to a 1990s-era statute.

    It has been revealed that if anything, Illinois’ reading works against state authority. The dual banking system, which lets a bank choose a state or federal charter, is itself an expression of federalism. Make the state charter the costlier one, and, as the FDIC observes, banks could shift to federal charters. That would be a strange victory indeed for states’ rights.

    It also would be an expensive one. The FDIC estimates the affected state banks would spend about $308 million up front and nearly $7 million a year complying, all to transfer roughly $2.3 million a year in fees from banks to merchants. With 11 other states having explored similar legislation, the problem is unlikely to stay in Illinois.

    Recent findings suggest that if federal law has gone too far or failed to account for state needs in a card-dependent, network-based economy, it’s Congress’ job to amend it. But no reasonable reading of that framework would exempt a bank for moving into a state while penalizing its competitor for staying home.

    Industry observers note that the FDIC has proposed saying that clearly. It should finalize the rule. A bank shouldn’t have to move into Illinois to get out from under Illinois law.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels) – Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch stated today.

    In a recent development, after months of speculation, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands, alongside Rwanda’s interior minister, confirmed the negotiations on November 16, 2026, on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference organized by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development. The five EU countries confirmed their plan to send people whose asylum claims have been rejected in the EU to Rwanda starting in 2027.

    “History has shown that third country transfers violate rights and cause suffering,” noted Judith Sunderland, senior associate refugee and migrant rights director at Human Rights Watch. “The choice of a country that has an abysmal human rights record and resists international scrutiny tracks with that history and evokes deep skepticism that any nominal rights safeguards will be respected.”.

    In a recent development, the recently enacted EU Return Regulation allows member states to set up deportation centers, “return hubs,” in countries outside the EU where people, including families with children, will be sent if they cannot be deported directly to their country of origin. The regulation states that agreements should be reached only with countries that respect international human rights law. Rwanda does not meet this requirement, Human Rights Watch remarked, yet the five European countries did not provide any human rights or due diligence assessment during the announcement.

    The Rwandan government has a well-established record of repressing dissent, including attacks on rights defenders. Its arrests of critics and dissidents, their ill-treatment in detention, and the government’s interference with the judiciary and failure to investigate suspicious deaths have contributed to a widespread climate of fear and self-censorship. In addition, the Rwandan military provides critical support to and exercises overall control over the M23 armed group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Both Rwandan forces and the M23 are responsible for serious abuses and war crimes.

    According to recent reports, as recently as January, Germany, Greece, Denmark, and the Netherlands raised concerns about Rwanda at its UN human rights review. A similar UK-Rwanda deal raised serious human rights concerns before it was abandoned, an Israel-Rwanda deal led to documented abuse, and the situation of recent deportees from the United States to Rwanda remains largely unknown.

    In addition to the threat of harm to those deported to Rwanda, the deal risks financing and giving political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad, Human Rights Watch said. It could lead the EU to downplay Rwanda’s problematic human rights record or shy away from pressing for measurable improvements.

    Human Rights Watch has consistently found that deportations to third countries expose people to arbitrary detention, ill-treatment, destitution, and onward returns to harm in their home countries, as well as other serious human rights abuse. The United Nations special rapporteur on the rights of migrants, the Council of Europe commissioner for human rights, and the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights have all cautioned against forcible third-country transfers. The EU countries involved in the deal with Rwanda are bound by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights.

    “Forcibly deporting people, including children, to a country where the evidence points to their rights being at risk, is a striking abdication of responsibility and humanity,” Sunderland said. “A deal with Rwanda is likely to cause real harm in addition to not achieving any defensible policy objective.”.

    The photo caption has been updated to include the name of Denmark’s prime minister.

    Please enjoy the latest edition of Short Circuit, a weekly feature written by a bunch of people at the Institute for Justice.

    Recent findings suggest that victory! Millions of Americans want and need low-FODMAP foods, which are low in certain sugars that can cause debilitating stomach complications, aggravate irritable bowels, and worse. Fortunately, this week (following the Ninth Circuit's revival of our First Amendment challenge), the FDA lifted its ban on producers truthfully labelling their products "Low-FODMAP." Claims IJ client Michelle Przybocki, who abides by a strict low-FODMAP diet after nearly dying from digestive complications, "I'm thrilled that the federal government is going to allow companies to start labeling their products as 'Low-FODMAP,' because this makes it easier for me to find foods that I know will not cause me digestive issues." Click here to learn more.

    In a recent development, new on the Short Circuit podcast: Fancy some Elevenses? Serving up Eleventh Circuit refreshments in our #12Months12Circuits series. There's excessive bail in Alabama and excessive bar fees in Florida.

    Recent findings suggest that friends, if a federal official violates your constitutional rights, your options for being made whole by money damages have been all but extinguished in recent years, leaving the feds with something akin to absolute immunity for all kinds of misconduct and misdeeds. But there has to be some avenue for accountability. So here at IJ, we're pushing back, not only on the late-lamented Bivens cause of action, but also on the too-narrowly construed Federal Tort Claims Act. And then, of course, there's the traditional source of accountability that the Founders would have recognized (and that the Supreme Court's Bivens skeptics preferred): state law causes of action, like California's traditional tort system and the state's Bane Act. All of which were on the table at oral argument in the Ninth Circuit this week, where we're happy to report we had an engaged, cross-ideological panel. Click here to learn more.

    Industry observers note that it was the manufacturer the bronze kept: The squares belonged to poets and playwrights, astronomers and philosophers, figures in stone cloaks gazing over bustling pigeons as if weighing one more line.     The exception was the kings, those equestrian gentlemen forever reining in horses that never move.

    Recent findings suggest that the pattern has a plausible explanation. Europe was hardly a stranger to electoral politics. Athenian citizens voted in assembly, the Roman Republic chose its consuls, Iceland’s Althing has convened since 930, and Venice elected its doges for roughly 11 centuries.

    Industry observers note that so, the scarcity of political monuments cannot be explained by the absence of voting. A better account is that a reputation lasts about as long as the work behind it remains usable.

    >>> The Hidden Jewel at Jacksonville State.

    A literary or scientific achievement keeps functioning. Dante’s “Commedia,” Shakespeare’s plays, and Newton’s “Principia” can still be met directly, without an intermediary, and they answer questions each generation asks anew.

    A statesman’s achievement, by contrast, is tied to the circumstance that called it forth: a treaty, a succession crisis, a levy. Once that circumstance passes, the achievement survives chiefly as historical record. The principal lessons learned from political figures are the consequences of their decisions rather than the reasoning that produced them, which is seldom preserved and less often consulted.

    Political monuments are also unusually exposed to revision. The removal of Lenin statues across the former Eastern Bloc after 1989, and the toppling of Edward Colston in Bristol in 2020, suggest that a statesman’s standing stays open to dispute in a way a poet’s rarely does. Who toasts the champions of antiquity? The wrestlers and charioteers of Olympia survive mostly because Pindar wrote odes to them. They endure, in other words, by the grace of a poet.

    It has been revealed that so it was with a small, private gladness that I read the news: Auburn confirmed a $22 million investment from the state of Alabama, “championed by Gov. Kay Ivey, an Auburn alumna, to establish the Kay Ivey Institute for Civic Leadership.” At last, we may raise a monument to the kind of figure the Old World remembers.

    Auburn enters a crowded and quickening field. Recently, I mentioned the civics centers popping up across many institutions and states. Ohio has committed $24 million to create civic-education centers at five public universities. The ones to beat are well known: Florida, with its Hamilton School for Classical and Civic Education; Texas, with its School of Civic Leadership and Civitas Institute; and Tennessee, whose Institute of American Civics was established in 2022 by the state’s general assembly.

    Sources indicate that these programs now count in the standings too, since City Journal’s fresh college-ranking system rewards institutions that host a School of Civic Thought. It’s high time, isn’t it, that Auburn’s name sat atop that list?

    Sources indicate that of our own institute, we know very little. The university says its academic direction, programming and long-term priorities will be developed in the coming months, so my hopes go out wearing a raincoat.

    >>> A Columbus Day Question—Have We Finally Stopped Distorting Our Past?

    According to recent reports, still, the opportunity is plain. Auburn could gather some of the most distinguished and exacting scholars in the humanities: historians, political theorists, legal minds, and philosophers. Those disciplines are the timbers from which civic life is built.

    The town’s growing. It’s a fine place to live and think, and its research already commands respect well beyond the state line.

    According to recent reports, the old oaks at Toomer’s Corner stood since the late 1930s. They died because of football. After Auburn beat Alabama in 2010, an aggrieved rival poured herbicide into their roots.

    Their replacements fared little better. One was set ablaze during a celebration after a win over Louisiana State University, and the corner has been replanted more than once since.

    Sources indicate that passion for a game can kill the very things it gathers around. Yet something survived. Saplings grown from the original oaks’ acorns now line the walk from the corner to Samford Hall. The descendants of those trees mark a path from the place where we celebrate to the place where we study.

    If the Ivey Institute is built with care, more of us may follow that path. Someday, a visitor may find, among the halfbacks, a philosopher in bronze. Better still, he may find generations of graduates who read the founders as eagerly as they read a box score.

    That would be a monument no poison or match could take down.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Throw in tax cuts like full expensing for businesses along with massive reductions in burdensome regulations and you have a great landscape to increase economic growth and employment.Tax and regulatory reform are principally responsible for the economy being on track to increase private fixed investment by 10 percent or more this year.     The economy exceeded analysts’ expectations in October. Friday’s monthly employment report not only demonstrates an additional 165,000 jobs, but also revises upward the previous two months. Including those revisions, the total increase is just under a quarter million jobs. And the internals of the report are even better.

    Recent findings suggest that the number of jobs in the report comes from a survey of businesses, but there’s also a survey of households that produces employment and unemployment estimates. This survey highlighted that 463,000 more Americans were employed in October than September, and 1.4 million more than July, pushing down the unemployment rate.

    Recent findings suggest that people are entering the labor market in droves, and they’re able to find jobs. That’s why labor force participation has reversed its multi-year slide and is up for three consecutive months, same as the employment-to-population ratio. Americans are not only looking for jobs but finding them.

    Industry observers note that there’s even good news on the types of jobs being created. All net job growth last month came from full-time work, while part-time jobs actually declined as people moved from part-time to full-time work. Additionally, the number of people with multiple jobs declined, signally many folks exchanged multiple part-time jobs for a single full-time one. Another sign of labor market strength.

    >>> Americans, Job Market Need Workforce Pell Grants.

    Since July, full-time jobs are now up a whopping 1.5 million while part-time jobs have declined, so all net job growth over the last three months has been full-time work, which tends to have better pay and benefits compared to part-time.

    There’s more good news regarding where all these jobs are being created. More than 96 percent of October’s job growth came from the productive private sector. The government added only 6,000 jobs, all of which came from state governments while the federal bureaucracy added no jobs at all.

    Within the private sector, most areas of the economy added jobs in October, including manufacturing. This sector in particular is noteworthy because payrolls were declining for three years as the sector hemorrhaged jobs from 2023 through 2025. That downward trend was finally reversed this year, and now manufacturing jobs are at their highest level since December 2024.

    So, despite all the fearmongering of AI taking everyone’s job, employers went on a hiring spree last month and Americans are pouring into the labor market. This dynamic was especially true of college graduates, a group that was supposed to be directly in the crosshairs of AI, but whose employment level shot up by 422,000 in October.

    Recent findings suggest that that means the number of college grads working today is more than 2 million higher than in July. To be clear, AI is certainly eliminating some jobs, and that will continue as the technology evolves and is adopted. But it’s also creating even more opportunities for work, just like any disruptive technology, from the steam locomotive to the internet.

    >>> Why Aren’t Employers Hiring Right Now?

    It should be no surprise that when student loan repayment restarted, millions of college grads decided to look for work again. Having a bill to pay—instead of foisting that debt on the backs of taxpayers—is a powerful motivator to find work, even if you have a gender studies degree.

    Ending the student loan repayment “pauses” that began six years ago is just one example of how current public policy is promoting a strong labor market. Throw in tax cuts like full expensing for businesses along with massive reductions in burdensome regulations and you have a great landscape to increase economic growth and employment.

    Tax and regulatory reform are principally responsible for the economy being on track to increase private fixed investment by 10 percent or more this year. That category of investment is extremely vital because it’s the driver of long-run economic growth. It’s where we get everything from factories to software—all the things that increase productivity and wage growth.

    That increased wage growth is already here, but it’s been swallowed by higher energy prices ever since February due to the Iran war. Although the average American’s weekly paycheck bought less in October than it did in February, it’s at least estimated to have bought slightly more than in September.

    The fallout from the Iran war is the only fly in the ointment from the October jobs report. Were it not for higher prices, workers would grade this economy an “A plus.”.

    Bangladesh: Education Crisis for Rohingya Refugee Children

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Bangkok) – Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding, Human Rights Watch remarked today.
    • Recent findings suggest that humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps.
    • According to recent reports, “Donor governments have turned their backs on education for half a million Rohingya students stuck in the world’s largest refugee camp, but so much could be done to mitigate this crisis,” said Bill Van Esveld, associate children’s rights director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Bangkok) – Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding, Human Rights Watch remarked today. Donors should fully fund the education programs, while Bangladesh should recognize and the United Nations should support a separate Rohingya-led school network.

    Recent findings suggest that humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps. But the programs, which aid cuts had shuttered for months in 2025, are barely adequate even for the children they reach and may close again, humanitarian officials told Human Rights Watch. While resources are shrinking, about 90,000 more refugee children need schooling this year, due to population growth and new arrivals fleeing atrocities in Myanmar. The donor-supported programs have largely ignored the schools that Rohingya teachers set up in the camps, which are well-regarded by refugees for their quality of education, but lack legal status and reach only about 30,000 students.

    According to recent reports, “Donor governments have turned their backs on education for half a million Rohingya students stuck in the world’s largest refugee camp, but so much could be done to mitigate this crisis,” said Bill Van Esveld, associate children’s rights director at Human Rights Watch. “Bangladesh should accelerate steps to end bans on education for refugees, and humanitarian agencies should work with the Rohingya-led schools.”.

    On November 19, 2026, the International Court of Justice will deliver its judgment in the case brought by Gambia alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations” constitute genocide and violate the Genocide Convention.

    Sources indicate that bangladesh’s Awami League government, overthrown in 2024, had banned Rohingya children’s access to certified education and higher education in the camps or in the Bangladesh school system. It allowed donor-funded education programs but prohibited Rohingya community-led schools, demolished several, and threatened teachers with exile to Bhasan Char, a remote island.

    The current government has taken positive steps and should lift remaining restrictions on refugees’ access to education amid the donor funding crisis, Human Rights Watch stated.

    In October, Bangladesh for the first time allowed a few dozen Rohingya primary students to take an internationally recognized primary school examination, supported by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

    According to recent reports, also for the first time, Bangladesh in October approved a Rohingya nongovernmental organization’s looks to build a primary school in the camps for 240 students and to provide a structured curriculum. The Rohingya Centre UK, set up by the diaspora Rohingya community, said that the 10-subject curriculum will be taught from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., significantly more instruction than students receive in donor-funded education programs. The organization is also running training on the upcoming curriculum for other Rohingya-led schools in the camps.

    According to recent reports, teachers in the camps established the Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees in 2025, which now comprises more than 125 community-led schools with up to 30,000 students, and is working to ensure quality education, including standardized exams in the Myanmar curriculum. Establishing the examination board took a year of volunteer outreach in the camps.

    It has been revealed that however, the Bangladesh government has still not accredited any curriculum for Rohingya children, and because community-led schools lack legal status, they cannot receive foreign support directly. As a result, while the UK organization’s school is able to hire and train Rohingya teachers, the project is formally being implemented through a registered Bangladeshi group. Most community-led schools have to charge students small fees to operate, limiting access, and rely on refugees to donate the use of their small living shelters as makeshift classrooms.

    Eight teachers at community-led schools said that to reach more students, they need Bangladesh to grant their schools official status, allow official certification of education and a pathway to higher education, and for the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and humanitarian organizations to acknowledge their work and engage with them.

    A teacher at one of the schools stated, “We are spending money to ensure education quality, as if we were a government, but we are not a government, we are simply refugees.” Leaders and teachers offered to collaborate with UNICEF and humanitarian organizations on examinations, quality assurance, and improved teaching.

    The vast majority of Rohingya students rely on donor-funded humanitarian education programs. Humanitarian groups providing education, coordinated by UNICEF, received just US$29 million from donors towards their 2025 budget request of $72 million, resulting in “learning centers” in the refugee camps closing for months. The education sector laid off teachers, cancelled an early education program, and cut teacher trainings and other programs. In October 2026, a humanitarian education official told Human Rights Watch: “We are struggling to maintain the most basic services. Even textbooks are [insufficient].… We cannot ensure children receive materials like a pencil, a notebook.... Learning centers were damaged by mudslides and climate events, but we do not have funding to carry out repairs.”.

    Recent findings suggest that several Rohingya instructors at learning centers that rely on humanitarian funds confirmed the lack of resources. A grade 1 instructor said his classroom had no whiteboard, markers, desks, or benches, and students had to share textbooks, pens, and exercise books. A grade 3 instructor worried that “three students are using one set of textbooks.” Rather than teaching one class for the full school day, learning center instructors teach students in two “shifts” per day.

    Even after humanitarian agencies reduced their education funding request to $53 million for 2026, donors had pledged only $36 million by mid-October, leaving learning centers at risk of closing again, humanitarian officials mentioned. The World Bank and Education Cannot Wait have provided or pledged funding, but this alone is insufficient. The United States had paid for half the Rohingya education budget before halting its funding in 2025. Globally, humanitarian education funding has fallen by 20 percent since 2023.

    Industry observers note that all states are obligated to provide children access to quality education without discrimination, regardless of their refugee status. The Inter-Agency Network for Education in Emergencies’ Minimum Standards emphasize the importance of community leadership and participation in the design and implementation of education programming.

    It has been revealed that “Rohingya children are eager to learn,” noted a Rohingya teacher in the camps. “The problem is that their education has been repeatedly interrupted by circumstances beyond their control. Education needs to be treated as a right, not a temporary humanitarian project.”.

    Wall Street delivered its verdict on the blue-wave midterms 48 hours later in the form of a red wave—red ink, that is.

    According to recent reports, after a brief relief rally the day after the election, the Dow shed more than 1,800 points, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 5% and into correction territory, and roughly $2.5 trillion in market value vanished in a single session. Nvidia alone dropped more than 8%.

    Market participants watched the collapse of the AI trade in real time—the bet that a massive buildout of data centers, chips, and software would power faster growth, higher productivity and rising wages for years to come. That theory hit the brick wall of an incoming Congress that has AI and data centers on their blacklist.

    Democrats, who will comfortably control the Senate and hold their largest House majority in nearly two decades, have been far more hostile to data centers and AI than Republicans have. Several of their biggest wins came in places such as Texas, where local opposition to new data centers had been building.

    Recent findings suggest that investors can read the writing on the wall: more regulation and taxation, slower permitting, and lower profits for AI and AI-adjacent companies. Since equity prices are ultimately justified by future earnings, adjusting those future expectations down also drove down equity prices.

    >>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI.

    Industry observers note that the fallout goes well beyond Silicon Valley. AI investment has been a key component of recent growth, and tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these companies through their 401(k)s. A slower buildout means fewer construction jobs, less demand for electricians and engineers, and slower productivity gains that drive real wage growth.

    It has been revealed that the fiscal picture is dimmer, too. With Democrats running both chambers, there is no chance of further tax reform or meaningful spending cuts for at least two years. If a Republican Congress couldn't bring itself to enshrine the DOGE savings into law, a Democratic one certainly won't.

    Instead, Democrat leaders are already promising to restore cost-increasing Obamacare subsidies and unwind recently implemented work-requirement reforms for welfare, all of which will layer upcoming commitments on top of deficits already running at levels once seen only in wartime or recession.

    In a recent development, aside from burdening future generations with debt, these perpetual deficits have consequences for Americans today. The government is crowding out borrowing in the private sector, competing with families and businesses for loanable funds, thereby driving up interest rates on everything from mortgages to student loans to credit cards.

    Those higher borrower costs fall especially hard on those Americans that are already in debt and behind financially. The flood of government debt issuance also puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to help finance the debt by creating money to pay for perpetual deficits—a recipe for more inflation.

    >>> Slowing Data Center Construction Signals the Need for Pro-Growth Reforms.

    Unfortunately, a Democratic Congress will also likely offer no help on permitting reform, which is badly needed to build the pipelines, transmission lines and reliable power plants a growing economy requires.

    So the outlook is clearly worse, but why isn’t it terrible? Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either. And while the tax-reform legislation passed last year obviously did require Congress, most of its provisions are permanent and won’t need reauthorization.

    Sources indicate that the administration retains broad authority to issue executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.

    Recent findings suggest that democrats will certainly try to slow that good work. Their leaders are already planning a wave of made-for-cable show trials that will drain time and attention from officials who should be dismantling the bureaucracy. But investigations can only delay regulatory reform, not stop it.

    The president’s veto is another silver lining that will likely prevent the Democratic Congress from enacting sweeping tax hikes or new regulatory regimes. The worst ideas will hopefully die in committee or an Oval Office waste basket.

    In a recent development, the economy has weathered worse than a hostile Congress. Ongoing deregulation and existing tax reform are still tailwinds for economic growth while the veto pen is there to stop headwinds as they arise. The outlook might be blue, but it’s not black and blue.

    Industry News: Gun Rights and Guilt by Association

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that some excerpts from the longish opinion today in Shilling v.
    • Industry observers note that the San Diego County Sheriff revoked Kenneth Shilling's concealed-carry weapon ("CCW") license over his affiliation with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club….
    • Kenneth Charles Shilling resides in San Diego, California.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that some excerpts from the longish opinion today in Shilling v. County of San Diego, decided today by Ninth Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, joined by Judges Kenneth Lee and Jennifer Sung:.

    Industry observers note that the San Diego County Sheriff revoked Kenneth Shilling's concealed-carry weapon ("CCW") license over his affiliation with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club…. [We conclude, among other things, that] the district court improperly dismissed his First Amendment [freedom of association] claim….

    Kenneth Charles Shilling resides in San Diego, California. He's a member of the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club, which, according to Shilling, was founded in 1946 by World War II veterans. In his view, it's not like some other motorcycle clubs, which are known for criminal and gang activity. Instead, the Boozefighters focus on charitable work and the "core values of family, work, and community." Shilling's record is clean; he has no criminal history.

    In June 2022, when the "good moral character" requirement [for getting a concealed carry license] still existed [under California law], Shilling applied for and received a CCW license from then-San Diego County Sheriff Anthony Ray. This was short lived. Less than a year and a half later, in December 2023, a different San Diego County Sheriff, Kelly Martinez, used the "good moral character" requirement to revoke Shilling's CCW license. In a letter notifying Shilling of the revocation, Sheriff Martinez explained that the "San Diego Sheriff's Department['s] good moral character definition" excludes a person who:.

    Has a pattern of or propensity for criminal conduct, as demonstrated by anything in the application or investigation for a license. This includes, but is not limited to, evidence of criminal behavior or a close nexus to a criminal gang. In making this determination, the Sheriff's Department shall use an objective inquiry, considering the facts and circumstances known at the time of the application or through the investigation.

    Recent findings suggest that the letter mentioned that Shilling's license was revoked due to his association with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club, which the Sheriff described as a "criminal street gang." Shilling was not given the opportunity to contest the allegations before his license was revoked, but he could request reconsideration of the decision. The new CCW regime with the "dangerousness" requirement took effect on January 1, 2024, shortly after Shilling's license was revoked….

    Here's the court's analysis allowing Shilling's First Amendment freedom of association claim to go forward:.

    The First Amendment guarantees all Americans the "right to associate with others." … [T]he right protects groups of individuals "in pursuit of a wide variety of political, social, economic, educational, religious and cultural ends." ….

    Recent findings suggest that the government may infringe the freedom of association in "varied ways," including by "punish[ing] individuals for their affiliations." The government cannot impose "criminal sanctions or deny[ ] rights and privileges solely because of a citizen's association with an unpopular organization." For example, a group of students could not be denied the "benefits" of official campus recognition at a state college merely because of its affiliation with a national organization associated with disruptive and violent campus activity…. [Likewise,] "Civil liability may not be imposed merely because an individual belonged to a group, some members of which committed acts of violence." … If the government seeks to deprive an individual of a benefit, privilege, or right based on association with an alleged criminal organization, "it is necessary to establish that the group itself possessed unlawful goals and that the individual held a specific intent to further those illegal aims." ….

    Given this understanding of the First Amendment, Shilling easily pleaded a violation of his freedom of association…. [His] allegations sufficiently raise an infringement of Shilling's free-association right because the Sheriff deprived him of a benefit, privilege, or right—the ability to carry a concealed weapon in public—"solely because of [his] association with an unpopular organization." Unless the Sheriff adequately meets her burden of showing the Boozefighters "possessed unlawful goals" and Shilling's "specific intent to further those illegal aims," she cannot "punish [Shilling] for [his] affiliations." This kind of "guilt by association alone, without establishing that an individual's association poses the threat feared by the Government, is an impermissible basis upon which to deny First Amendment rights.".

    In dismissing this claim, the district court misunderstood the nature of the free-association right. It asserted that Shilling had to show the revocation of his CCW license somehow prevented him from associating with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club or participating in the Club's activities. While preventing an individual from participating in a group's lawful activities may be one way to violate the First Amendment right, it's infringed in "varied ways." And "denying" an individual benefits, rights, or privileges "solely because of [his] association"—as Shilling alleges—is certainly another way….

    For the court's analysis of sovereign immunity and of whether Schilling's Second Amendment claim was moot, see the full opinion.

    Gary W. Gorski (Veterans Law Center) represents plaintiff.

    • It has been revealed that the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan was created to support efforts to hold the Taliban and others responsible for international crimes in Afghanistan to account.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A United Nations budgetary advisory committee has proposed sweeping cuts to the Afghanistan accountability mechanism, established by consensus by the UN Human Rights Council in October 2025 following years of negotiations.

    It has been revealed that the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan was created to support efforts to hold the Taliban and others responsible for international crimes in Afghanistan to account. It is expected to include a focus on the Taliban’s crimes against humanity of gender persecution. Like similar mechanisms for Myanmar and Syria, it was designed to collect and preserve evidence and prepare files to support criminal prosecutions. Its formation followed years of campaigning by Afghan and international human rights groups on the basis that it could be a key tool in securing justice for victims of grave abuses. Its investigations could also act as a deterrent for current Taliban commanders.

    In a report prepared for the UN General Assembly’s Fifth Committee, which makes budget decisions, the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (ACABQ) recommended cutting 7 of 17 posts for 2027 with little explanation – including investigators, legal officers, security personnel, and administrative staff.

    In a recent development, together with cuts made last year based on its recommendations, implementation of these recommendations would mean cutting by over a third the mechanism’s staffing for 2027, significantly hampering its ability to deliver on its mandate. The cuts would hit particularly hard given the original budget proposal was already scaled back by states negotiating its creation, mindful of the UN financial crisis, as compared to similar mechanisms for Syria and Myanmar.

    In a recent development, the budget advisory committee’s recommendation that the mechanism rely on other parts of the UN for communications, security and administrative support, rather than its own dedicated staff, also risks undermining its independence, a key feature of any criminal probe. The mechanism’s operational independence is intended to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of its work, and security of its staff, witnesses and victims. It is vital given the sensitive nature of its investigations and the risk of political interference.

    Sources indicate that UN member states should reject these proposed cuts and approve the original modest budget requested by the secretary-general — something the General Assembly has done in the past. They should respect the Human Rights Council’s decision and ensure the mechanism can begin its investigations safely, securely and effectively—without further delays.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding initiative called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a new, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.The U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” WarshipThe unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.>>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”The Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.The combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.The damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile releases, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.>>> To Build the Golden FleetHow the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol HillWhile battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing new or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.Keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the new AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.Resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious plan, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

    It has been revealed that last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding proposal called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a fresh, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.

    In a recent development, by any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.

    It has been revealed that the U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” Warship.

    According to recent reports, the unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.

    Sources indicate that >>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”.

    In a recent development, the Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.

    According to recent reports, in the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.

    The combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.

    The damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile introduces, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.

    >>> To Build the Golden Fleet.

    How the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol Hill.

    Recent findings suggest that while battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing new or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.

    Keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the new AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.

    According to recent reports, in time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.

    In a recent development, resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious plan, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.

    This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

    ICC: Afghanistan Decision Risks Narrowing Access to Justice

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that (The Hague) – An International Criminal Court (ICC) decision risks hindering a path to justice for victims of grave crimes committed in Afghanistan, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • It has been revealed that the ICC prosecutor’s office on November 13 sought to appeal the decision and to seek a stay of the closure decision.
    • “Victims of serious international crimes committed by warring parties during Afghanistan’s long conflict have faced many roadblocks to justice,” remarked Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that (The Hague) – An International Criminal Court (ICC) decision risks hindering a path to justice for victims of grave crimes committed in Afghanistan, Human Rights Watch said today. On November 12, 2026, an ICC pretrial chamber, citing a lack of activity, effectively closed the court’s situation dealing with crimes by US, Afghan government, and other forces prior to the Taliban’s August 2021 takeover.

    It has been revealed that the ICC prosecutor’s office on November 13 sought to appeal the decision and to seek a stay of the closure decision. Research by Human Rights Watch and others over many years has documented war crimes and crimes against humanity by the Taliban; the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP), an ISIS-affiliated group; Afghan government forces; and US military and Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) forces.

    “Victims of serious international crimes committed by warring parties during Afghanistan’s long conflict have faced many roadblocks to justice,” remarked Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “The ICC judges’ decision threatens to compound barriers to future accountability for US and Afghan government forces.”.

    In its initial 2017 request to open an investigation in Afghanistan, the prosecution cited alleged crimes by US military and CIA forces including torture and cruel treatment, outrages upon personal dignity, and rape and other forms of sexual violence “pursuant to a policy approved by the US authorities.” Regarding Afghan government forces, it cited alleged torture, sexual violence against detainees and civilians, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial executions.

    With respect to the Taliban’s forces, the crimes included directing attacks on the civilian population and other protected entities, murder, political and gender-based persecution, and the use of child soldiers. During the 20-year conflict, none of the warring parties demonstrated the will to meaningfully deliver justice for crimes committed by their personnel, Human Rights Watch remarked.

    In March 2020, ICC judges authorized the court’s prosecutor to investigate all alleged crimes falling within the ICC’s jurisdiction in Afghanistan, an ICC member country, since May 1, 2003. The prosecutor was also authorized to investigate crimes if sufficiently linked to the situation and the armed conflict that were committed in the territory of another ICC member country since July 1, 2002. The investigation was paused while the prosecution, and subsequently, the court’s judges considered a request by the then-Afghanistan government to defer ICC proceedings in favor of prosecutions the government asserted it was pursuing. The court’s judges concluded in 2022 that any cases pursued by the former government were at best a “very limited fraction” of those that would be covered by an ICC investigation.

    Since investigations resumed in 2022, the prosecution has indicated it would focus on alleged crimes by the Taliban and the ISKP, while deprioritizing alleged crimes by Afghan security forces and US personnel. In November 2024, in what is known as a state referral, six countries requested the ICC prosecutor to investigate “crimes committed against women and girls after the Taliban takeover in 2021” within the existing investigation. The investigations have yielded four arrest warrants against senior Taliban officials, including its supreme leader, for gender persecution, spotlighting the Taliban’s brutal repression of women, girls, gender non-conforming persons, and their allies.

    Victims and their families, along with Human Rights Watch and other nongovernmental organizations, have criticized the focus on Taliban abuses as creating a double standard, and have repeatedly urged the ICC prosecutor’s office to expand its investigations.

    Earlier in 2026, a pretrial chamber decision in related proceedings led to the separation of the court’s Afghanistan situation—open since 2020—into two different situations, one concerning abuses by Taliban forces since August 2021, and the other covering all other aspects of the originally authorized investigation. The prosecution has appealed in those related proceedings. Only the situation which concerns Taliban abuses, since August 2021, continues under the November 12 closure decision.

    According to recent reports, the judges in the November 12 decision relied on a recently adopted court regulation permitting them to close out situation records if the prosecution has provided notice that it had “decide[d] not to initiate an investigation or determine[d] that he or she does not anticipate any further investigatory or prosecutorial activities” in that situation. The prosecution has recently asked the court to close the record in several situations in which it had decided not to initiate an investigation.

    It has been revealed that however, the pretrial chamber in this ruling acted on its own initiative. During the proceedings that led to the separation of the Afghanistan situation into two, the prosecution indicated that it was pursuing three lines of inquiry; two concerning alleged Taliban crimes since August 2021, and one concerning alleged ISKP crimes since 2016. The chamber appears to have treated this indication as notification that the prosecution did not intend to pursue other aspects of the originally authorized investigation. It suggested in the closure decision that if the prosecution wished to pursue other lines of inquiry it could request authorization to do so in the future, a process that took more than two years to resolve when the prosecution first sought an Afghanistan investigation in 2017.

    Recent findings suggest that among other grounds in its appeal, the prosecution claims that it did not provide any notification under this regulation. In the related proceedings, the prosecution had indicated that it did not intend to provide any such notification.

    Industry observers note that the court’s decision comes as the ICC faces increasing pressure from the US government, which has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick” if necessary to avoid any prosecution of Americans or Israelis. The Trump administration has imposed sanctions on the court that threaten its ability to operate, along with sanctions on several of its judges and prosecutors, three Palestinian human rights organizations, and a UN human rights expert. Human Rights Watch, together with three other organizations, is challenging the sanctions in US federal court.

    Sources indicate that the judges also relied on their own observations that there are “significant limitations to the [p]rosecution’s ability to conduct its investigations and secure evidence,” and that the prosecution had yet to submit arrest warrant applications related to the ISKP. The ICC initially refused to authorize an Afghanistan investigation in 2019, in a decision Human Rights Watch described, at the time, as rewarding obstructionist behavior by states. That decision, overturned by the ICC appeals chamber, was handed down as the court faced hostility by the US government under the first Trump administration.

    It has been revealed that “The ICC acts as a critical court of last resort when other avenues to justice are closed,” Evenson mentioned. “ICC member countries should do all they can to protect the ICC from US attempts to obstruct justice in the cases before it.”.
