    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Note, the release has been updated to include a quote from the National Security Division.
    • An eight-count superseding indictment was unsealed today charging Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), two U.S.
    • According to recent reports, “Anyone who prepares a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government,” noted Attorney General Todd Blanche.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Note, the release has been updated to include a quote from the National Security Division.

    An eight-count superseding indictment was unsealed today charging Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs), including their involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States, and a September 2026 terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where American armed forces were stationed.

    According to recent reports, “Anyone who prepares a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government,” noted Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The defendants listed in the indictment allegedly supported two foreign terrorist organizations, and al-Saadi allegedly coordinated with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted terrorist plot. This Department of Justice will continue dismantling terrorist networks and protecting the American people from terrorist organizations.”.

    Industry observers note that “This eight-count indictment reveals the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the U.S., including one plot that was recently prevented at RAF Fairfield, a British Royal Air Force Base where American forces were stationed,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “According to the indictment, one of the subjects is behind bars awaiting trial yet he allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence. To date, the subjects have been allegedly involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (“IRGC”), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations. This FBI will use all our resources to detect and stop such terrorist attacks as we’ve done the last 21 months – with over 1,300 terrorists disrupted and nearly 7,000 Foreign Terrorist Organization related arrests, up 1,057%. All those who threaten our homeland will get the message – justice will find you.”.

    It has been revealed that “Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy,” mentioned Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “No matter where they are in the world, the National Security Division of the Department of Justice will pursue those who target American citizens and American interests. My thanks go out to the prosecutors and law enforcement partners for their work on this case.”.

    “As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” stated U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of Fresh York. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas. The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real. Our Office will not stop working to address and disrupt this threat, and to prosecute those responsible.”.

    In a recent development, according to the allegations contained in the superseding indictment and other court filings: Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and al-Hassani allegedly conspired to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the United States on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, both of which are FTOs. Most recently, in approximately September 2026, al-Hassani allegedly orchestrated a terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base (RAF Fairford) in Fairford, United Kingdom (the “RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot”), which at the time of the attempted attack, housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel.

    Sources indicate that al-Hassani and Mohajeri, both of whom were in Iran at the time of the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot, allegedly relied on a network of contacts in the United Kingdom. Al-Saadi, who was imprisoned and awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges in the Southern District of New York, attempted to coordinate with al-Hassani and Mohajeri from jail by passing coded messages through third parties.

    Recent findings suggest that al-Saadi, a longtime operative of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, was charged in May for working with and on behalf of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, as well as other FTOs, for his involvement in planning and promoting approximately 18 terrorist attacks in Europe; and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in Newly introduced York. The picture below demonstrates al-Saadi in front of an array of machineguns in a conference room with a map of the United States on the wall next to a list of “legitimate targets” (redacted here) identifying former and current U.S. officials.

    As alleged, among the individuals with whom al-Saadi worked to facilitate and carry out the European Terrorist Attacks were Mohajeri and al-Hassani. Mohajeri is an Iranian national and operative of the IRGC who coordinated with al-Saadi and al-Hassani to carry out those terrorist attacks with the IRGC’s backing. Al-Hassani, who is originally from Iraq, used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out terrorist attacks in the United Kingdom.

    The European Terrorist Attacks were carried out in the name of a purportedly new terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which is a front for Kata’ib Hizballah and other FTOs. Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the United Kingdom, the most of any European country. The attacks involved arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual U.S.-British citizen.

    Recent findings suggest that al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and Al-Hassani were allegedly personally involved in planning many of the European Terrorist Attacks, and al-Saadi and Mohajeri helped create and publish online propaganda videos of these attacks. For example, on or about April 6, Mohajeri and al-Hassani planned attacks while together in a room in Iraq with a map of London displayed on a computer screen. In a video of that meeting, al-Hassani told Mohajeri, “we need to get focused on London.”  An image of the video is below, with Mohajeri on the right and al-Hassani on the left. HAYI then claimed responsibility for six terrorist attacks that occurred in and around London starting approximately one week later.

    Recent findings suggest that on or about April 17, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri allegedly directed an individual to carry out one of the European Terrorist Attacks in real time. Specifically, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri, along with others, were in a room watching a FaceTime video with the individual who was carrying out the attack, which was projected onto a large screen against the background of the HAYI logo. Al-Hassani directed the perpetrators’ actions, including by instructing the individual on the other end of the call to execute the attack and directing that individual to take a lighter and “light one in your hand,” “light it,” and “throw the fourth one.” Al-Saadi recorded the attack in real time, while Mohajeri recorded al-Hassani and al-Saadi in the room as they directed the attack. A still image from Mohajeri’s recording, showing al-Saadi (circled in red) and al-Hassani (circled in green), as they directed and filmed the attack, is below.

    The next day, on or about April 18, al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London, with the HAYI logo projected on the background of al-Hassani’s screen. During the video call, al-Hassani directed the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The person on the video then lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at a building. An image from the video is shown below.

    In March and April — overlapping with the time that al-Saadi was co-located in Iraq with Mohajeri and al-Hassani, planning the European Terrorist Attacks — al-Saadi allegedly attempted to coordinate and carry out terrorist attacks in the United States, including by targeting a synagogue in Manhattan.

    According to recent reports, on or about May 1, following the European Terrorist Attacks, al-Saadi was arrested abroad and subsequently transferred to the custody of the United States to face prosecution. Al-Saadi has been in federal custody since his arrival in the United States. For approximately four months following al-Saadi’s arrest, there were no additional attacks attributable to al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and al-Hassani.

    In August, however, al-Hassani allegedly directed and paid associates in the United Kingdom to conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani paid one individual (Individual-1) to perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford’s perimeter and al-Hassani subsequently received videos of the area surrounding the base. In later communications with al-Hassani, Individual-1 referred to him as “Ali.”.

    Sources indicate that in September, al-Hassani also tasked and paid several individuals to help him prepare for the plot, including by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. At al-Hassani’s urging, those individuals commissioned custom decals that they affixed to the vans to create the appearance that they were used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

    It has been revealed that on Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base. That day, al-Hassani was in frequent communication with the van drivers, helping to coordinate their movements and directing them where to drive. At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route. Al-Hassani communicated with the drivers and occupants of the vans both before and after encountering the security checkpoint. In the early morning hours of Sept. 27, law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three white vans to which the fuel delivery business logos were affixed and arrested the occupants.

    Sources indicate that while in prison in New York awaiting trial, al-Saadi has had phone calls with his immediate family members located in Iraq. As alleged, al-Saadi used those calls to pass coded messages to Mohajeri and al-Hassani in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

    Recent findings suggest that for example, in June and July, al-Saadi allegedly spoke with his mother and sister about Mohajeri. During those calls, they referred to Mohajeri by various aliases, including “Abbas, Abu Daniel” and “Sayyid Abbas.”  Al-Saadi also told his family members that he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass along messages to Mohajeri about “work,” a term al-Saadi regularly used to describe terrorist activity, including on social media posts and in discussions with Mohajeri about partnering to conduct terrorist attacks. On one of those calls, al-Saadi also asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and asked her whether it had been cancelled or just put on pause. Al-Saadi’s sister responded that “it isn’t cancelled.”.

    It has been revealed that on or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi once again spoke with his immediate family by phone. On the call, al-Saadi allegedly inquired about how al-Hassani, whom al-Saadi referred to as “Ali,” was doing. Al-Saadi’s family informed al-Saadi that “Ali” had been transferred to the “International Section.”  Al-Saadi then allegedly instructed his family to “give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it.”  As described above, three days later, al-Hassani orchestrated the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

    Al-Saadi, 32, is a citizen of Iraq and Iran. Mohajeri, 48, is a citizen of Iran. Al-Hassani, 35, is a citizen of Iraq. A chart containing the names, charges, and minimum and maximum penalties for the defendants is set forth below.

    The Justice Department praised the outstanding investigative work of the FBI’s Fresh York Joint Terrorism Task Force, which consists of investigators and analysts from the FBI, the NYPD, and over 50 other federal, state, and local agencies, and the FBI Washington Field Office, Counterterrorism Division, as well as the assistance of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, Counterterrorism Section, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the NYPD, the New York State Police, and the Department of State.

    Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jeffrey W. Coyle, Sarah L. Kushner, David J. Robles, and Chelsea L. Scism for the Southern District of Latest York are prosecuting the case, with assistance from James Donnelly and Paul Casey of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

    Industry observers note that A superseding indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

    • According to a Monday story from Law.com, Meredith Arfa, the assistant U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 17, 2026, 12:39 pm CST.

    According to recent reports, federal prosecutors urged jurors Monday to convict Chinese technology company Huawei, arguing that the company had grown by repeatedly committing crimes. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    Federal prosecutors urged jurors Monday to convict Chinese technology organization Huawei, arguing during closing statements in the ongoing 11-week trial involving trade secrets theft and sanctions evasion that the company had grown by repeatedly committing crimes.

    According to a Monday story from Law.com, Meredith Arfa, the assistant U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Newly introduced York, told jurors that Huawei spent two decades pursuing growth “by any means possible.”.

    To illustrate the trade secrets allegations, Arfa played a video of a former Huawei employee removing part of Tappy, T-Mobile’s robot for testing phone touchscreens, from the carrier’s lab. She also demonstrated side-by-side images of Cisco’s and Huawei’s router source code, saying the two matched exactly—down to an engineer’s stray comment mentioning someone named “Bob.”.

    “This simply couldn’t happen without copying,” Arfa stated in her summation.

    She further alleged that Huawei managers encouraged theft by paying bonuses for obtaining confidential competitor information, and that employees boasted about it on an internal forum.

    In a recent development, on the sanctions compliance allegations, prosecutors remarked Huawei secretly controlled Skycom, a subsidiary that supplied sensitive technology to Iran’s government. Arfa said the firm repeatedly lied about owning Skycom. She also pointed to admissions by Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer, who signed a deferred prosecution agreement after spending three years under house arrest. Meng acknowledged that Skycom’s operations violated U.S. sanctions, and that she misled HSBC, Huawei’s primary bank, about its compliance, Arfa noted.

    Huawei, one of the largest telecommunications companies in the world, denies the allegations, contending that the case rests on the independent actions of rogue employees who were disciplined.

    Sources indicate that the government declared the case in 2019. The company is represented by Jenner & Block, Sidley Austin and Steptoe.

    Justice Department Confirms Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.
    • Recent findings suggest that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” stated Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M.
    • “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” stated Assistant Attorney General A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

    Recent findings suggest that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” stated Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement shows that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”.

    “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” stated Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division swiftly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”.

    In a recent development, “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”.

    Industry observers note that “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”.

    “The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” mentioned FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”.

    “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” said Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”.

    Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California.

    Recent findings suggest that today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California revealed the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

    North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

    During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the upcoming victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

    In a recent development, the North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

    It has been revealed that the FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

    The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

    The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance.

    Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

    Recent findings suggest that efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

    The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the agentic era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe AI agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice and agentic AI applications for OpenAI, Salesforce, Spotify, Meta, and tens of thousands of other developers, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    We're hiring a Solutions Architect (Pre-Sales) to be the technical partner to the engineers and enterprises building on LiveKit.

    You'll work alongside an account executive to understand what a customer is trying to build, design the right architecture, and bring it to life with live demos and proofs-of-concept — guiding teams from first conversation to production.

    This role is ideal for someone who loves to build, is energized by talking with other engineers, and takes pride in turning a hard technical problem into something that just works. Real-time voice and video is visceral — latency, quality, and reliability are felt, not read about — so the best conversations include something live. You'll collaborate closely with our Sales, Engineering, Product teams to win technical decisions and to make sure what you hear in the field informs how we build.

    love to build and solve the most challenging customer problems with LiveKit.

    have a curious mind with a continuous desire to learn and improve.

    enjoy demoing and presenting, whether to a room or engineer, to a CTO or at a conference.

    have a team first mentality, seeking to lift others around you as you progress in your career.

    Partner with an account executive as the technical lead on strategic deals — from discovery and architecture design through demos, POCs, and technical decisions.

    Advise customers on cloud architecture and deployment across self-hosted and LiveKit Cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure).

    Build live demos and reference applications — voice agents, video pipelines, telephony integrations — tailored to each customer's use case, and reusable by the wider team.

    Scope and run proofs-of-concept against clear, shared success criteria, guiding customers all the way to production.

    Reason with customers about connectivity, infrastructure, and end-to-end latency to design for scale and reliability.

    Create technical content — blog posts, guides, webinars, and conference talks — that helps developers and enterprises build with LiveKit.

    Act as the technical enabler for your region's pod, and share field insight with Product and Engineering to help shape the roadmap.

    4+ years in solutions architecture, sales engineering, or a customer-facing engineering role (or equivalent hands-on engineering experience with strong customer instincts).

    Hands-on experience with at least one major cloud provider (AWS, GCP, or Azure) — you can architect, deploy, and debug real applications.

    Comfortable with the modern deployment toolchain: containers, Kubernetes, infrastructure-as-code, and networking fundamentals (load balancing, DNS, firewalls/NAT).

    Able to reason about connectivity, infrastructure, and latency end to end — how architecture, network path, compute, co-location, and model choice shape the AI agentic experiences of today.

    Strong programming ability in at least one of our core SDK languages — Python, TypeScript/Node, or Go.

    A clear communicator who can demo, present, and write for technical audiences.

    Working knowledge of real-time media protocols and their latency/quality trade-offs (WebRTC, RTP/SRTP, WebSockets).

    Familiarity with the AI voice stack: STT/TTS providers, LLM integration, speech-to-speech models, turn detection, and telephony/SIP.

    Experience speaking at meetups or conferences, or a track record of technical writing or open-source contributions.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    LiveKit is an equal opportunity employer and does not discriminate on the basis of any characteristic protected by applicable law. If you require a reasonable accommodation during the application or interview process, please contact recruiting@livekit.io.

    • NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname.
    • Recent findings suggest that in a federal complaint filed Tuesday in the Southern District of New York, James said he has been known as “Bron” since he was a young basketball standout in Ohio.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname.

    Recent findings suggest that in a federal complaint filed Tuesday in the Southern District of New York, James said he has been known as “Bron” since he was a young basketball standout in Ohio. He alleges that PlayVision and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, seek “to trade on” his “valuable name and reputation” by naming their app Bron.

    In a recent development, there is no other connection between the word and the defendants or any other feature of their app, James alleges. He also argues in the complaint that when the defendants launched a marketing campaign for the Bron app earlier this month, they used a video advertisement that incorporated an artificial intelligence-generated version of him.

    Industry observers note that “The AI-generated version of Mr. James sits in an NBA-style locker room wearing a basketball jersey bearing Mr. James’s nickname, ‘Bron,’ above the number ‘23’—a number associated with Mr. James and the one he currently wears on the Philadelphia 76ers—with physical traits that mimic Mr. James, down to his identifiable tattoos,” according to the complaint.

    It has been revealed that “Speaking in Mr. James’s voice, the AI-generated Mr. James scrolls through wagers on other NBA players in defendants’ Bron app,” the complaint continues. “The ad then urges viewers to ‘scroll to bet.’”.

    The lawsuit seeks damages and an injunction preventing the defendants from using the “Bron” name; James’ name, image and likeness; and voice.

    Courthouse News Service has additional reporting.

    A representative for Bron did not respond to the publication’s request for comment.

    #44216. The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1728 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.
    • This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known.
    • The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

    This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

    First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

    Recent findings suggest that this process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal matter in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

    Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

    Sources indicate that as noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

    Recent findings suggest that nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an crucial concern of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

    This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an matter that has been turned down one or more times.

    Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

    Sources indicate that the answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

    But much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 states the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an important matter of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

    Just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

    The cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

    And the justices rarely discuss it. In his newly introduced book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

    Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

    Many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

    The clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

    Caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

    Recent findings suggest that question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

    Recent findings suggest that the number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

    Oddly, no one seems to know why.

    There are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

    Sources indicate that these interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

    In a recent development, different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer new laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

    Industry observers note that it is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a manufacturer based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the problem (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

    Question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

    In a recent development, the Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal issues, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

    Sources indicate that A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

    The process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

    Steve Wermiel is a professor of practice at American University Washington College of Law, where he has taught a seminar on the Supreme Court for nearly three decades.

    Recommended Citation: Stephen Wermiel, The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 12, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-sometimes-straightforward-sometimes-befuddling-certiorari-process/.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that uscreen is the video monetization platform for businesses building recurring revenue from video content. Our customers replace a patchwork stack of separate hosting, community, courses, email, and app vendors with one branded experience across web, mobile, and TV.

    The platform is only half of it. We believe growth requires behavior, not just software. Customers don't stall because a feature is missing. They stall because they priced wrong, never built an email list, or launched an offer nobody wanted. Coaching is how we fix that, and it's part of the product rather than an add-on.

    You own a segment, and you run it like a growth marketer.

    We have a cohort of smaller video businesses where retention is not where it should be. Nobody owns it today. You will. The revenue that stays in that segment, and the revenue that grows inside it, is yours.

    According to recent reports, this is a coaching role for someone with a growth marketer's mindset. We wouldn't hire a demand gen marketer who couldn't analyze the state of the business and figure out what's needed, and we won't hire a coach who can't either. You'll look at a customer's business the way an owner would: where the revenue comes from, where it leaks, and what to do next. You pull your own numbers to get there. When a customer needs a custom report to answer a growth question, you build it yourself.

    It's a one-to-many job. Your cohort is larger than a 1:1 book, so the work is designing coaching that scales: cohort programs, group sessions, office hours, and triggered outreach when the data says a business is drifting. You'll build that motion rather than inherit it.

    According to recent reports, success is measured in dollars: gross revenue retention in your cohort first, expansion second. Not tickets closed, not calls booked.

    A coach with a growth marketer's mindset. Maybe you've run growth or demand gen for a small business, built your own audience, or coached founders through their numbers. You understand how a membership business makes money, you pull your own analytics to see what's working, and you're comfortable doing it in front of a client. What matters is that you can find the real constraint in a business, then sit with the operator and say the honest thing.

    Benefits may vary depending on location and local regulations. Final eligibility and coverage details will be shared during the hiring process.

    • In all of these cases, including this one, the policies at concern are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    According to recent reports, on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case is one of several in recent years dealing with magnet school admissions policies. While prior cases addressed the constitutional permissibility of changes to selection criteria at some of the nation’s most sought after public high schools like the Thomas Jefferson High School in northern Virginia and Stuyvesant High School and Bronx High School of Science in Latest York City, this case addresses whether changes to selection criteria for middle school magnet programs in Montgomery County, Maryland violates the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment.

    In all of these cases, including this one, the policies at concern are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process. As a result, the Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard is not directly relevant. In that case, the court held that using race as an explicit factor in the admissions process was unconstitutional.

    Sources indicate that at issue in this case is a change from one facially neutral admissions policy to another. During the pandemic, the school adopted the so-called “Pandemic Initiative.” Under the Pandemic Plan, all students are considered for admission to magnet schools if they meet minimum grade requirements and if their locally compared state assessment scores exceed a cut-off. Admission is then determined by a lottery from among those students who meet these requirements. Because schools in the region differ in their racial composition, basing admissions decisions on how well students score relative to other students in their same school ultimately affects the demographic composition of admitted students. AFEF claims that the Pandemic Plan violates equal protection because Montgomery County adopted it in order to change the racial demographics of the magnet schools and the plan had the effect of decreasing the share of Asian-American and white students.

    According to the approach used by all of the courts evaluating magnet school admission practices, these facially neutral policies only violate equal protection if they are adopted for an impermissible reason (the intent element) and produce a discriminatory effect (the effect element). In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the district court found that the plaintiff had not alleged facts sufficient to satisfy either prong and so the school board’s motion to dismiss was granted. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit affirmed on the grounds that the district court properly evaluated whether there was a discriminatory effect.

    When and why facially neutral policies violate equal protection is a hotly contested glitch. Consider first the intent element. While all agree that the intention to exclude members of a particular racial group is invidious, there is disagreement about whether the intent to increase racial diversity is also impermissible. The Supreme Court has not yet directly ruled on this vital issue and will not do so in this case. The cert grant in AFEF v. Montgomery County focuses only on the second element: the discriminatory effect. In particular, the Supreme Court limited its grant of AFEF’s petition to the following question: “Whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.”.

    In a recent development, this framing of the question roughly tracks the debate in the circuits between two different ways of showing discriminatory effect. In order to illustrate, let’s set aside the intent prong and assume it has been satisfied, either because the policy was actually adopted in order to reduce the percentage of Asian or white students in the magnet schools (though this fact is in dispute) or because the intention to increase the racial diversity of the schools is an impermissible intention (though this legal claim is contested). According to the 4th Circuit in Coalition for TJ v. Fairfax County and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit in Boston Parent Coalition for Academic Excellence Corp. v. School Committee for the City of Boston, the effect element would be satisfied if a lower percentage of Asian or white students are admitted than applied. For example, if Asian students represent 30% of the applicant pool but only 20% of the admitted class, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. However, if 40% of the admitted class are Asian, then no discriminatory effect would be found because Asian students would in this case constitute a higher percentage of the admitted class than their 30% share in the applicant pool. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, both the district court and the 4th Circuit followed this approach.

    By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit in Sargent v. School District of Philadelphia, the dissenting judge in Coalition for TJ, and Justice Samuel Alito in his dissent from the denial of cert. in that case, assess discriminatory effect differently. Rather than compare the percentage of admitted students of the race alleged to be intentionally excluded to their percentage in the wider applicant pool, these jurists look to see if there has been a decrease in the percentage of admitted students of this race under the newly introduced policy as compared to the prior policy. When a meaningful decrease is present, this constitutes a discriminatory effect. For example, if 50% of the admitted class were Asian under the prior policy and 40% are Asian under the new policy, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. And this would be so even if Asian students are still “overrepresented” in the sense that the percentage admitted is higher than their percentage of the applicant pool (30% in this example). In an article evaluating each of these approaches, we call this second approach the “Before-After Comparison” or “BAC,” and we call the first approach the “Population Comparison” or “PC.”.

    In a recent development, yet both the PC and the BAC, as means of assessing discriminatory effect, have significant flaws. Let’s begin with the PC – the test used by the 4th and 1st Circuits. Recall that because the doctrine requires both impermissible intent and a discriminatory effect, it requires something more than just the fact that a policy is chosen for an invidious reason. The PC would effectively allow deliberate attempts to exclude Asians so long as they do well enough overall and do not fall below their share of the applicant pool. That seems problematic.

    Next consider the BAC, the test adopted by the 3rd Circuit, on which the discriminatory effect prong is satisfied only if the percentage of Asian students declines under the upcoming policy. This test puts a strong thumb on the scale in favor of existing policies, whatever their merits, since sticking with the same policy is unlikely to result in major changes in the demographics of who is admitted. Thus a decision to keep things the same will evade scrutiny. And this is so even when maintaining a policy is done for uncontroversially bad reasons (say, because the existing policy is known to admit fewer Asian students, for example). In addition, the test is oversensitive to any changes in policy, since such changes are likely to lead to demographic shifts among the admitted students and thereby trigger a decrease for some group. While it is true that there will only be an equal protection violation if the school board at glitch intended this decrease, it remains the case that any change at all is risky because the effect element will likely always be satisfied for some group. For both these reasons, the BAC privileges the status quo and makes change difficult by making the status quo policy the normative baseline.

    The use of the term “aggregate” in the question on which certiorari was granted suggests that the court might think that the PC approach is flawed because it looks at how groups are treated rather than at how individuals are treated. And indeed it does. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the discriminatory effect element would be satisfied (using the PC) if the percentage of Asian and white students admitted was lower than the percentage of these groups among the fifth-grade students in the county. But the BAC is no different in this respect. It too looks at how a racial group fares under the Pandemic Plan. The BAC would find discriminatory effect if the percentage of Asian students admitted under the Pandemic Plan is less than the percentage admitted under the approach that preceded it. In other words, both tests for discriminatory effect focus on how the racial groups who are alleged to be the target of the invidious intentions fare as groups.

    Can either of these tests be reframed in ways that focus on how an individual is treated, rather than how members of her racial group are treated? After all, equal protection doctrine has long emphasized that the clause protects individuals rather than groups. Unfortunately, this is not easy to do. If a school uses race to decide which students to admit, it makes sense to say that a student’s race played a role in how she was treated. Facially neutral policies are different, however. Consider a simple and familiar facially neutral policy. Suppose a school board decides to admit the top 2% of each middle school to its coveted magnet high school. Suppose also that it does so, at least in part, to increase the racial diversity of the magnet school. Because there are more black and Latino students in some middle schools and more Asian and white students in others, this policy then produces a magnet school class that has a significant number of students of all races, let us suppose. Now consider an Asian student who is denied admissions because she is not in the top 2% of her middle school class. Has she been denied admission “because of her race?”.

    One answer to this question could be simply “no.” Any student rejected by the admissions policy suffers a harm. It is this harm that gives the student standing to sue. But this rejection is not based on the student’s race when the school’s admissions policy is facially neutral. If this is correct (and if aggregate tests are out), then the court’s only option is to jettison the effect prong of the claim altogether. Were the court to take this route, facially neutral laws or policies would violate equal protection solely on the grounds that they were adopted with invidious intent.

    The U.S. Court of Appeal for the 2nd Circuit attempts a different approach. It uses the BAC to explain how individual students have suffered a discriminatory effect under a facially neutral policy. In Chinese American Citizens Alliance of Greater Newly introduced York v. Adams, the percentage of Asian students admitted under the challenged admissions policy remained higher than their percentage in the applicant pool (thus failing to satisfy the PC in its aggregate form) and also did not decrease as compared to the prior admissions policy (thus failing to satisfy the BAC in its aggregate form). Yet the 2nd Circuit held that the effect element “can be satisfied by proof of an adverse harm to one or more individuals based on their race that has resulted from that discriminatory law or policy” (emphasis added). But the crucial question remains: in what way were the rejected Asian students rejected “because of their race” when race did not affect these decisions since the policy is facially neutral? The 2nd Circuit answers that question by referring to the fact that these students were “qualified for admission on an individual basis under the previous criteria" (emphasis added). In other words, in the view of the 2nd Circuit, if a new policy is adopted to exclude Asian students, then those Asian students who would have been admitted under the previous policy are denied admission because of their race.

    According to recent reports, this approach can be understood as an attempt to make the BAC individualized: the court here is determining whether a student’s rejection constitutes a distinctively discriminatory harm by drawing a comparison with how she would have fared under the previous policy. If this approach works (which we are agnostic about) for the BAC, a similar approach can be tailored for the PC as well. Here is how that would go. If a facially neutral policy was adopted in order to exclude Asian students and that policy is one under which Asian students are admitted at lower rates than students of other races, then each Asian student subject to that policy is subject to a policy that makes it harder for them to be admitted than it is for students of other races. On this view, each Asian student denied admission using this policy is then denied admission based on their race.

    Thus, both tests can be articulated such that they capture a way that individual students are rejected based on their race. For this reason, the court should not choose one approach over the other on the grounds that one frames the injury in individual terms and the other looks at how groups are treated.

    This leaves the court with two options. First, as mentioned earlier, it could jettison the effect prong of the claim entirely and conclude that bad intentions alone render a facially neutral admissions policy impermissible. Doing so would put more pressure on the importance of answering the question of what intentions are invidious and, in particular, whether the intent to increase racial diversity is itself unconstitutional. Alternatively, the court must confront the question of discriminatory harm head-on and assess whether the BAC or PC provides the better account of it.

    Industry observers note that deborah Hellman is the Robert E. Scott Distinguished Professor of Law and the Honorable Albert V. Bryan Jr. ’50 Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, as well as Director of their Center for Law & Philosophy.

    Lily Hu is an Assistant Professor of Philosophy at Yale University and also a contributing editor at Boston Review.

    Sources indicate that recommended Citation: Deborah Hellman & Lily Hu , What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 12, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/what-is-a-discriminatory-effect-the-montgomery-county-case-and-unpacking-when-schools-may-try-fo/.

    Penn Law professor’s lawsuit is free speech case, not employment discrimination, 3rd Circuit states

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (201 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006.
    • In a recent development, the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S.
    • The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial problems was more of a First Amendment issue, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006. (Photo by Jeffrey M. Vinocur, CC-BY-SA-3.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

    In a recent development, the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Philadelphia noted Tuesday.

    The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial problems was more of a First Amendment issue, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.

    In her brief, Wax, a white Jewish woman, stated that Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act prohibit discrimination “on the ground of race” and “on the basis of race,” respectively, differing them from Title VII.

    She argued that the the University of Pennsylvania had an alleged double standard, allowing faculty and students to participate in what she called antisemitic demonstrations against Israel without consequences but punishing her for her commentary on race.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase is the backend of choice for a growing wave of AI-native builders, and we're deepening structured partnerships with the platforms they build on top of — Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable. These partners' teams are talking to thousands of developers and agents who need exactly what we build—a full backend platform with Postgres at the core—without the vendor lock-in. This is an opportunity to get Supabase in front of the right partner SAs and make us the default recommendation for a modern, AI-ready backend.

    We’re looking for a Platform Solutions Architect to join our Success Team and help embed Supabase into the Solutions and Engineering communities with AI Builders.

    You’ll work closely with Partner Solutions Architects and Partner Engineers at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, helping us proactively identify builder problems where Supabase is the right solution and closing the gap between partner intent and real developer outcomes. This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions of AI-native apps and agents.

    In this role, you’ll focus on three core pillars:.

    Build deep relationships with Technical counterparts at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, focusing initially on defined use cases and agent/app-migration motions.

    Develop and deliver technical workshops, training materials, and enablement content to give partner SAs the fluency to position Supabase.

    Create demos, integration guides, and reference architectures that make Supabase’s fit with Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable immediately legible.

    Partner with SAs at these companies on active opportunities to move deals forward and feeding technical pipeline intelligence back to the alliance lead.

    Resolve blockers for partner SAs working on Supabase implementations to maintain their credibility with the builders they support.

    Troubleshoot complex integration scenarios and turn solutions into reusable assets.

    Maintain a close feedback loop with Supabase product and engineering teams to ensure technical guidance reflects the latest platform capabilities.

    Measure success through co-sell opportunities sourced, influenced deals, and SA enablement metrics across the Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable partnerships.

    Write technical blog posts and case studies that demonstrate real-world Supabase implementations built on Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable.

    It has been revealed that represent Supabase at conferences, meetups, and partner-sponsored events (e.g. Anthropic and OpenAI dev days, Vercel Ship, Lovable community events).

    Develop video content and interactive learning experiences to reduce the "time-to-fluency" for partner SAs.

    Recent findings suggest that have 5+ years of experience in technical roles with deep hands-on experience building on modern AI infrastructure. Previous experience working at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, Lovable (or a similar AI builder platform) or as a partner to one is required.

    Understand how partner SAs at AI builder platforms are incentivized, how they make recommendations, and how the partner ecosystem influences developer decisions.

    Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences, explaining complex concepts with ease.

    Have a strong technical foundation in PostgreSQL, APIs, and modern development frameworks like React and Next.js, plus fluency with AI/agent tooling (LLM APIs, MCP, agent frameworks).

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving promptly to build a playbook from scratch.

    Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers building the next generation of AI-native products.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    It has been revealed that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    The major Trump cases that might come back to SCOTUS
